content: Tinea infections, caused by dermatophyte fungi, are common skin conditions affecting 10% to 20% of the global population. The specific sites of infection vary depending on geographical, environmental, and cultural factors, as well as the fungal species involved. Tinea corporis, also known as ringworm, and tinea cruris, commonly referred to as jock itch, are frequently encountered by primary care physicians and dermatologists. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation and can be confirmed through microscopy or fungal culture. A variety of topical antifungal agents are used to treat these superficial fungal infections, but the relative efficacy of these treatments remains uncertain. To evaluate the effectiveness of topical antifungal therapies for tinea cruris and tinea corporis, a systematic review was conducted. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving patients with confirmed dermatophyte infections of the body or groin. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases up to August 13, 2013, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS. Additional sources, such as trial registries and reference lists, were also examined. A total of 364 records were identified, and 129 studies involving 18,086 participants met the inclusion criteria. However, half of these studies were judged to have a high risk of bias, while the remainder had an unclear risk of bias. The studies evaluated a wide range of topical antifungal treatments, with azoles being the most commonly studied class of drugs. Treatment durations ranged from one week to two months, with most studies lasting two to four weeks. Follow-up periods varied from one week to six months. Unfortunately, 63 studies lacked usable or retrievable data, often due to the absence of separate data for different types of tinea infections. The primary outcomes assessed in the studies included mycological cure (elimination of the fungus) and clinical cure (resolution of symptoms). Adverse effects were also reported, though less than half of the studies evaluated relapse rates, and very few assessed the time to clinical cure or patient-reported outcomes. Pooled data from five studies showed that terbinafine was significantly more effective than placebo in achieving clinical cure, with a risk ratio (RR) of 4.51 (95% confidence interval [CI] 3.10 to 6.56) and a number needed to treat (NNT) of 3 (95% CI 2 to 4). However, the quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as low. Mycological cure rates for terbinafine could not be pooled due to substantial heterogeneity among studies. Naftifine 1% was also found to be more effective than placebo in achieving mycological cure, with a pooled RR of 2.38 (95% CI 1.80 to 3.14) and an NNT of 3 (95% CI 2 to 4) across three studies. The quality of evidence for this outcome was also rated as low. In one study, naftifine 1% demonstrated superior clinical cure rates compared to placebo (RR 2.42, 95% CI 1.41 to 4.16, NNT 3, 95% CI 2 to 5), but the evidence quality was again low. Clotrimazole 1% was shown to be more effective than placebo in achieving mycological cure, with a pooled RR of 2.87 (95% CI 2.28 to 3.62) and an NNT of 2 (95% CI 2 to 3) across two studies. Comparisons between different classes of antifungal treatments revealed no significant difference in mycological cure rates between azoles and benzylamines (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.07), though the quality of evidence was low. Data heterogeneity prevented pooling for comparisons between azoles and allylamines. Combination creams containing azoles and steroids were slightly more effective in achieving clinical cure immediately after treatment compared to azoles alone (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.84, NNT 6, 95% CI 5 to 13). However, there was no difference in mycological cure rates (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.05). The quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low for clinical cure and low for mycological cure. Overall, all treatments appeared to be effective, but most comparisons were based on single studies. There was no evidence to suggest differences in cure rates between tinea cruris and tinea corporis. Adverse effects were minimal, primarily consisting of irritation and burning, and were infrequently reported. The evidence for relapse rates and patient-centered outcomes, such as satisfaction with treatment, was insufficient. The review concluded that terbinafine and naftifine are effective treatments for tinea cruris and tinea corporis, with mild and infrequent adverse effects. However, many of the included studies were over 20 years old and had a high or unclear risk of bias. While azoles also demonstrated efficacy, most were evaluated in single studies. There is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of Whitfield’s ointment, a commonly used treatment. Although combination creams containing antifungals and steroids showed higher clinical cure rates, their use is not currently recommended in clinical guidelines due to very low-quality evidence. Further high-quality, adequately powered trials focusing on patient-centered outcomes are needed to guide treatment decisions.
